You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 44

# The Weight of What He Carried Home

Marcus Tan is a 46-year-old Filipino-American firefighter who has spent the better part of two decades running toward danger. His colleagues at the station describe him as steady, methodical, the kind of man who can walk into a burning building without his hands shaking. What they do not know is that for the past three years, those same hands tremble every morning before his shift begins.

Before joining the fire department, Marcus spent fourteen months as a volunteer relief worker in a conflict zone in Mindanao in the southern Philippines, where he had family roots and a conviction that he could do something meaningful. He was thirty-three years old. He distributed food and medical supplies to displaced families, worked alongside local aid organizations, and learned quickly that the line between civilian life and active conflict was almost nonexistent. He witnessed artillery strikes on villages he had walked through the day before. He helped carry bodies — some of them children — from the rubble of a school that had been shelled overnight. One afternoon, a convoy he had been scheduled to travel with was ambushed. He had stayed behind that day because of a fever. Three people he knew were killed.

He returned to the United States telling himself he had processed it. He enrolled in firefighter training, married, had a son, built a life that looked, from the outside, entirely intact. For years, he believed his own story.

The unraveling began three years ago when his fire station responded to a structural collapse following an industrial explosion. Marcus was part of the extraction team. In the dust and the chaos, with concrete overhead and the sound of a child crying somewhere beneath the rubble, something inside him broke open without warning. He finished the rescue. He always finishes. But afterward, sitting in the apparatus bay still in his gear, he could not account for the previous forty minutes. He had been somewhere else entirely — back in Mindanao, in the dust, lifting a small body that had no weight left in it.

Since then, the past has become unreliable in a specific and exhausting way. It does not stay where he put it. He wakes at three in the morning with his heart hammering, certain he can smell smoke that isn't there, certain someone is dying and it is his fault. He has learned to lie still in the dark and wait for his nervous system to understand where he is, a process that can take twenty minutes or more. His ex-wife, Elena, noticed the sleeplessness and the distance long before he did. The divorce was finalized eighteen months ago. He tells himself it was mutual. He knows it was not.

At the station, Marcus manages by controlling everything he can. He is the first to arrive and the last to leave. He volunteers for extra shifts because the structure keeps the intrusive thoughts at bay, and because being home alone in his apartment has become something close to unbearable. He avoids the break room when his younger colleagues watch news footage from conflict zones on their phones. He has rerouted his commute to avoid a particular stretch of road where a billboard for a military charity shows a photograph of rubble that looks, in a specific quality of morning light, exactly like something he has tried for thirteen years not to see.

He does not drink. He is careful about that. His father drank, and Marcus has always understood, with a kind of grim clarity, exactly where that road goes.

What he will say, if you ask him directly, is that he is fine. That he has seen worse. That other people have it harder. He says this with complete sincerity, and with the particular confidence of a man who has spent his entire adult life being the person other people lean on when everything is falling apart. The idea that he might be allowed to fall apart himself has not yet fully formed in his mind. It is forming now, slowly, in the space between sessions, in the pauses before he answers questions he has never been asked before.
